notes: Food for home consumption is exempt.
Alcohol is taxed at the general rate, on top of per-gallon excise taxes left out here (liquor over 22% $3.60, 14% to 22% $1.30, up to 14% 70 cents, beer 16 cents).

Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at the general rate, on top of excise taxes left out here ($1.80 a pack of cigarettes; other tobacco by its wholesale price, premium cigars at most 50 cents each).
Household supplies: diapers (for children and adults) are exempt from January 1, 2025 to December 31, 2050 (2024 Question 5), which is not taken out here.
Personal care products: feminine hygiene products are exempt from January 1, 2019 to December 31, 2028 (2018 Question 2), which is not taken out here.
Barber and beauty services, laundry and dry cleaning, and auto repair labor: not taxed (FTA 2017 survey answer).

Motor fuel is exempt from the sales tax and pays per-gallon taxes instead: 33 cents in most counties (23 cents state, 9 cents county option and 1 cent), 28 cents in Esmeralda, Eureka, Lincoln and Storey counties, and more in Clark and Washoe counties, which index theirs (about 62.75 cents in all in Clark in fiscal 2027); left out here.

Hotel stays pay the sales tax plus county and city room taxes (in unincorporated Clark County, where the Strip is: 13.38% in the primary gaming corridor, 13% elsewhere in the school district area, 12.5% outside it and 10.5% more than 35 miles out, by Clark County tables; 13% in the city of Las Vegas, as reported; 13% or 13.5% in Reno and Sparks plus a nightly surcharge downtown; 11% in Carson City); not counted here.
Admission to live entertainment at venues holding 200 or more pays a 9% live entertainment tax instead; not counted here.

Nevada has no sales tax holiday for the general public; Nevada National Guard members and their families can claim a refund of the sales tax on purchases made October 30 to November 1, 2026 (Department of Taxation), not reflected here.
gaps: Nevada's 6.85% statewide rate is used as the state rate, following the state's own description of it, but only 2% of it goes to the State General Fund: 2.6% is the Local School Support Tax and 2.25% the city-county relief taxes. County add-ons in 13 of the 17 counties (to 7.1%-8.375%) are local; every county's rate matches the Department of Taxation's return form (REV-F013A, version 2025.1).
Nevada has no city sales taxes. The tourism improvement districts (NRS 271A) in the rate files charge their county's rate; they keep a share of the sales tax collected inside them instead.

programs: Redevelopment areas are mapped for Las Vegas (Redevelopment Areas 1, 2 and 3; Area 1 runs to 2046 after its extension), Reno (Redevelopment Districts 1 and 2), Carson City, Elko, Douglas County and Henderson (its five: Cornerstone, Downtown, Eastside, Lakemoor Canyon and Tuscany, from the city's open-data layer, 2019), and Reno's downtown business improvement district. North Las Vegas', Mesquite's, Sparks' and Boulder City's have no published maps and aren't shown, nor are the tourism improvement districts (NRS 271A) in Las Vegas, Reno, Sparks and Verdi, which keep a share of the sales tax collected inside them but charge the county's rate. Nevada Main Street's programs (among them Boulder City, Henderson, Las Vegas, Mesquite, Reno, Sparks, Ely, Tonopah and Virginia City) have no map.

warn.text: Clark County draws many visitors (Las Vegas and the Strip), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (2.5%) and its 642 lodging places (0.3 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, since a resort's few very large hotels count as only a handful of lodging places, though 31 of its 535 tracts (the Strip, downtown Las Vegas, Mesquite, Laughlin and Mount Charleston among them) are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Amargosa Valley's page is built from a census tract it shares with Beatty; that tract's flag as a visitor economy rests on 9 lodging places (4.1 per 1,000 residents), mostly Beatty's motels near Death Valley, so read that flag with care.

Battle Mountain may be flagged as a visitor economy only because of its motels along Interstate 80 (6 lodging places, 3.0 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers and mine workers rather than tourists, so read that flag with care.

Carlin may be flagged as a visitor economy only because of its motels along Interstate 80 (5 lodging places, 2.4 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers and mine workers rather than tourists, so read that flag with care.

Elko's flag as a visitor economy rests on its 35 hotels and motels (2.4 per 1,000 residents), which serve Interstate 80 travelers and gold-mining work travel as well as visitors, so read that flag with care.

Hawthorne may be flagged as a visitor economy only because of its motels on US 95 (7 lodging places, 2.4 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers and the Army depot more than tourists, so read that flag with care.

Las Vegas draws many visitors (downtown casinos and Fremont Street), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (1.6%) and its 121 lodging places (0.2 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs over the city as a whole, though 4 of its 152 tracts, among them the downtown casino tract, are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

McGill's page is built from a census tract it shares with Baker; that tract's flag as a visitor economy rests on 5 lodging places (3.4 per 1,000 residents) near Great Basin National Park, not in McGill, so read that flag with care.

Paradise draws many visitors (the Las Vegas Strip), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (4.5%) and its 239 lodging places (1.2 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs over the place as a whole, since a resort's few very large hotels count as only a handful of lodging places, though 9 of its 55 tracts, among them the Strip's own tract (85 lodging places for 1,680 residents), are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Reno draws many visitors (its casinos and nearby Lake Tahoe), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (1.1%) and its 129 lodging places (0.5 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs over the city as a whole, since a resort's few very large hotels count as only a handful of lodging places, though 7 of its 77 tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.
Wells may be flagged as a visitor economy only because of its motels along Interstate 80 (12 lodging places, 5.1 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers passing through, so read that flag with care.

West Wendover draws many visitors (its casinos on the Utah line), but the census tract its page is built from, which it shares with Montello, isn't flagged as a visitor economy: the tract's seasonal homes (3.1%) and its 3 lodging places (0.6 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, since a resort's few very large hotels count as only a handful of lodging places. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Winchester draws many visitors (the north end of the Las Vegas Strip), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (8.8%) and its 50 lodging places (1.5 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs over the place as a whole, since a resort's few very large hotels count as only a handful of lodging places, though 3 of its 9 tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.
